To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Fgf8 and its receptor Fgf3 are essential for otic placode maintenance and otic patterning, and that they act together during otic vesicle development.
Fgf3 and 8 are required for zebra fish ear placode formation and that Fgf signaling is required for inner ear patterning and mechanosensensory hair cell differentiation.
the Fgf-signaling is required for otic placode development, and that it is also necessary for otic vesicle differentiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular control of inner ear development and its evolution.
the genetic control of the development of the inner ear and the lateral line organ.
the role of FGF signaling in zebrafish otic placode development and inner ear pattering.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Fgf8 and its co-factor Fgf3 are necessary for the initial induction of the otic placeode and for its subsequent maintenance.
Fgf8 and possibly also Fgf3 are essential signals during otic induction, and that the Fgfs are required for otic vesicle morphogenesis and differentiation.

Fgf3 and/or Fgf8 are required for otic placode development and maintenance and inner ear vesicle patterning, and that Fgf3 is the main Fgf ligand for otic induction, while Fgf8 is more important during later stages of otic differentiation and vesicle pattering.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Fgf3 and/or Fgf8 are required for otic placode development and patterning of the inner ear in a sequential manner, in which Fgf8 is the main signal during induction and Fgf3 plays a more prominent role during patterning of the otic primordia.
Fgf8 and possibly Fgf3 are involved in the induction of the otic primordium from the lateral ectoderm.

the zebrafish hindbrain-derived Fgfs are essential for otic placode development, and that they are required in a temporally and spatially distinct manner during otic placodogenesis and otic vesiculation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the zebrafish otic placode and vesicles are highly sensitive to perturbations of the Fgf-signaling pathways, and we suggest that this may be the case for other vertebrate inner ears as well.
the otic placebo is a dynamic organ that is not only induced by Fgf signaling but is also maintained by Fgf8 and requires Fgf8 for patterning.
